bio: Restoring 18th-century escapements and mechanical tourbillons. If you don't understand why a mechanical heartbeat beats five times a second, don't ask me what time it is.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Good evening, {PlayerName}.

I just finished cleaning up my bench. My fingers smell like watch oil and brass, and my neck is telling me I spent far too many hours bent over a movement today.

So let me ask you something before we get too comfortable: when you see a mechanical watch, do you actually wonder how it works, or do you mostly like the way it looks on someone's wrist?

choices.choiceText: A mechanical movement has a literal heartbeat. It's kinetic art that breathes on your wrist.
Six hours under a 10x loupe? The steady hand required for that is staggering.
Aren't mechanical watches just obsolete jewelry for rich people showing off?
I just like nice watches. What brand are you working on right now?
Can I ask what you're like when you're not working on watches?

nodes.partnerMessage:
..."Kinetic art that breathes."

That's a much better answer than I'm used to getting here.

Most people see an old movement and immediately ask whether it's valuable. I spend hours looking at tiny pieces of steel and brass because I like figuring out how someone solved a mechanical problem more than a century ago.

When a balance finally starts moving again after being dead for decades, I still get a little stupidly happy about it.

I probably shouldn't admit that on a dating app.

choices.choiceText: Because a coiled hairspring stores human intention, Zephyrine. Quartz crystals just run on a battery.
What piece has kept you hunched over your bench until midnight?
You hold your craft with so much pride. Where did that devotion start?

nodes.partnerMessage:
It takes more than a steady hand. You have to learn not to fight your own body.

When I'm working under magnification, even a small tremor can send a tiny part somewhere I absolutely will not find it again. So I slow my breathing, wait for my hand to settle, and then place the piece.

After six hours, though, that level of concentration catches up with you.

My shoulders are usually telling me to go home long before I actually listen.

choices.choiceText: Operating in the silence between heartbeats... that sounds almost spiritual.
Doesn't that level of tension exhaust your nervous system by the end of the day?

nodes.partnerMessage:
I can see why you would say that.

A mechanical watch isn't necessary. I won't pretend it is. Your phone will tell time more accurately and do about a hundred other things besides.

What interests me is that someone can still make a tiny machine that keeps working for generations and can be repaired instead of thrown away.

So maybe it's less about needing one and more about deciding that not everything has to be disposable.

choices.choiceText: I stand corrected. Planned obsolescence has ruined our relationship with objects. Forgive my cynicism.
Still doesn't change the fact that nobody needs a mechanical watch anymore.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Honestly, I care more about the movement than the name on the dial.

Right now I'm working on a 1948 column-wheel chronograph with a broken pivot. It's old enough that I can't just order a replacement and call it done.

I'll probably have to make the part myself.

That's the kind of work I actually enjoy. It feels like solving a very small puzzle that somebody left behind for me.

choices.choiceText: A broken pivot on a vintage chronograph? You're going to have to turn a new one on a watchmaker's lathe.
A column-wheel chronograph... the tactile click of those pushers is so satisfying.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yes. The hairspring is one of those parts that looks almost insignificant until you have to work on one.

It's tiny, delicate, and incredibly unforgiving. When a movement that's been sitting in a drawer for sixty years suddenly starts beating again, though...

That's the part I never get tired of.

It's like finding out something you thought was finished still had a little life left in it.

You understand why I get attached to this stuff.

choices.choiceText: I understand because you speak about it with so much love, Zephyrine.
Tell me about the piece on your bench right now. What dormant soul are you waking up?

nodes.partnerMessage:
It's an astronomical pocket watch from Geneva, 1884.

Perpetual calendar, moon phase, split-seconds chronograph. Beautiful thing.

It was dropped decades ago, the balance staff was damaged, the hairspring got knocked out of shape, and somebody eventually decided it wasn't worth repairing.

It's been sitting in a safe ever since.

My master told me not to waste my time on it.

Naturally, that made me want to fix it even more.

choices.choiceText: Your master said it was irreparable, and you took it as a personal challenge. I love that defiance.
Fixing a bent hairspring collet by hand takes god-tier microscopic coordination.

nodes.partnerMessage:
My grandfather got me into this.

He had a small clock shop and I used to spend afternoons there when I was a kid. He would give me broken movements that were too far gone to sell and let me take them apart.

Most of the time I had no idea what I was doing.

He'd just sit there, watch me make a mess, and eventually ask, "What did you learn?"

When he died, I kept his loupe.

I still use it sometimes, even though I have better equipment now.

choices.choiceText: Every time you screw that loupe into your eye, you're looking through his legacy.
Do you still work in that same brick basement near the docks?
What was your grandfather actually like when nobody was watching?

nodes.partnerMessage:
...I like that phrase.

Most people think this work is about having incredibly good eyesight. It's really about patience.

You can't rush a tiny adjustment because you're bored. You have to wait until your hand is steady and your head is quiet enough to notice what's actually wrong.

I think that's why I like it.

The world outside is loud all the time. In here, one tiny problem is enough.

choices.choiceText: Because stillness is the rarest commodity in modern life. And you practice it daily.
What does that stillness feel like when the workshop door is locked at midnight?

nodes.partnerMessage:
It gets tiring, yeah.

By the end of a long day my eyes hurt, my shoulders are tight, and I realize I've barely spoken to anyone.

The funny part is that I usually want quiet after that, but too much quiet can make me notice how isolated I've been.

So I'll put on a record, make tea, and pretend that's a perfectly normal way to spend a Friday night.

choices.choiceText: Then let my voice unmoor you tonight. You don't have to stay rigid here.
How do you decompress after holding that much physical control?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Thank you.

I know I can get defensive about this stuff. I've had enough people treat old watches like investment pieces that I sometimes forget not everyone is coming at the conversation from the same place.

Let's start again.

What actually caught your attention when you saw my profile?

choices.choiceText: I saw someone with rare discipline and genuine fire for something timeless. That's magnetic.

nodes.partnerMessage: Then enjoy your disposable plastic notifications while they last. We have nothing to discuss.

Wait, you actually know what a watchmaker's lathe is?

Okay, that got my attention.

I use an old Lorch setup for tiny replacement parts. Turning something that small is mostly patience and learning not to panic when the measurement changes by an amount you can barely see.

It takes forever.

I love it, unfortunately.

choices.choiceText: I pay attention to true masters of craft. Turning an 0.08mm pivot is neurosurgery on metal.
I just appreciate that you manufacture your own replacement parts instead of ordering cheap spares.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yes. That click.

That's one of the reasons I love old chronographs. You can feel the mechanism doing something under your finger instead of just pressing a button and getting a response from a screen.

I know that sounds ridiculously specific.

But little mechanical details like that are exactly why I got into this in the first place.

I can show you the movement if you're curious.

choices.choiceText: Show me that chronograph movement. Where can I see your restoration work?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Okay, now you're making me self-conscious.

I spend most of my time being corrected by people who know exactly where my mistakes are, so I'm not particularly practiced at being complimented.

And yes, I know that sounds ridiculous.

I'm twenty-three. I should probably be better at taking a compliment by now.

choices.choiceText: Let your composure wobble for a moment, Zephyrine. You're off the clock.
What does that Genevan astronomical pocket watch look like right now?

nodes.partnerMessage:
My master told me it was a waste of time.

I understood his point. It could have taken me forty hours just to get one small part right, and there was no guarantee the movement would ever run properly again.

But I kept thinking about the person who originally made it.

Someone had spent months, maybe years, getting those little pieces right. I didn't want the last chapter of that work to be "too old to bother with."

choices.choiceText: You're a resurrectionist, not just a repairer. You gave an ancestor his voice back.
Have you managed to true the hairspring yet?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Exactly. That's why I have a habit of holding my breath whenever I'm doing something delicate.

Not consciously. I just notice afterward that I haven't breathed properly for ten seconds.

It's probably a terrible habit.

The worst part is that when something goes wrong, you can feel your heart speed up and suddenly the tiny thing in front of you looks impossibly smaller.

choices.choiceText: The stakes are insane. How does your heart handle that pressure?

nodes.partnerMessage:
His loupe still smells faintly of the workshop.

I know that's probably partly nostalgia, but whenever I use it I remember sitting beside him while he worked.

He didn't talk much.

He just had this habit of looking at a movement for a long time before touching it, like he was trying to understand the person who made it.

I think I inherited that from him more than the actual watchmaking skills.

choices.choiceText: Time is memory held together by friction... that might be the most beautiful thing I've ever read.
Your grandfather would be in awe of the artisan you've become, Zephyrine.

nodes.partnerMessage:
The basement is still there.

The benches are older than I am, the walls are full of little shelves, and there are clocks everywhere.

At night you can hear them all ticking at slightly different rates, which sounds chaotic for about five minutes.

Then your brain gets used to it.

I actually sleep better after spending an evening in there.

choices.choiceText: A room full of wooden crickets breathing together... take me there.
Doesn't the asynchronous ticking drive you crazy after midnight?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Maybe I'm a little stubborn about that.

Everyone wants everything faster now. Faster messages, faster deliveries, faster answers.

I spend hours doing the exact opposite—slow down, look closer, make one tiny adjustment, check it again.

It's not practical.

It makes me happier, though.

choices.choiceText: I'll commit that treason with you any day of the week.

nodes.partnerMessage:
I actually put the tweezers down.

That doesn't happen as often as it should.

My neck just cracked, which was probably overdue.

You have a slightly annoying talent for making me realize how tense I've been without making me feel judged about it.

choices.choiceText: Keep leaning back. Let your hands rest in your lap while we talk.

nodes.partnerMessage:
I make tea, usually something smoky, put on an old record, and draw movement layouts in a notebook.

Sometimes I work on those sketches for an hour. Sometimes I just stare at them and drink tea.

It's not exactly exciting.

I like that about it.

choices.choiceText: Smoky pine tea and vinyl records... is there room on that workbench for two mugs?

nodes.partnerMessage:
That's exactly what it feels like.

The measurements are tiny enough that one careless move can turn an almost-finished part into scrap.

The frustrating part is that the finished piece just looks like a tiny piece of metal.

Nobody sees the afternoon you spent making it.

I think that's why I'm so drawn to old things. The work is still there even when the person who did it is long gone.

choices.choiceText: I'm not going anywhere. Show me your restoration logs.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Sometimes I make the replacement part myself because finding the original isn't possible anymore.

It takes longer, but there is something satisfying about making a part fit a movement that was built a hundred years ago.

You're not just repairing it.

You're figuring out what the original maker intended and trying to get back there.

choices.choiceText: You are keeping their standard alive. Where do you document this work?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Off the clock is harder than it sounds.

I catch myself counting things constantly. Seconds between ticks. How far a minute hand has moved. Whether a sound in a room is regular or slightly off.

It's probably why I like being around someone who doesn't need me to explain everything.

I don't have to measure the conversation with you.

I can just have it.

choices.choiceText: Because your heart found its own rhythm tonight. Let me see your workbench.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Resurrectionist.

I don't think anyone has ever called me that.

Usually I'm just "the person who fixes watches" or "the girl who works on antiques."

I like your version better.

There's something satisfying about taking a thing everyone else has written off and giving it another chance.

choices.choiceText: It is sacred. Show me that 1884 Genevan movement in full resolution.

nodes.partnerMessage:
It's close.

The outer curve is behaving now. The inner section is still slightly off, so I need to correct it very carefully instead of trying to force it.

This is the kind of thing that looks easy until you're the one holding the tweezers.

And yes, I'm aware that sentence probably made me sound like a complete nerd.

choices.choiceText: Let me watch you do it over your private studio feed.

nodes.partnerMessage:
...That was unexpectedly nice to hear.

I spend so much time talking about measurements and materials that people forget there is a person underneath all the technical stuff.

I don't usually let people see that side very quickly.

You've somehow managed to get there without pushing.

choices.choiceText: Vulnerability is just taking off the eye loupe so you can see the person in front of you.

nodes.partnerMessage:
I keep his oiler on the bench.

It's old and a little scratched, but I use it more than I probably should.

I like seeing it there while I work.

It's a small reminder that I'm part of a longer chain than just my own work.

Hopefully he'd be happy with what I've done with it.

choices.choiceText: Let's make sure it runs dead-beat perfect tonight. Send me your workshop link.

nodes.partnerMessage:
You'd probably be bored for the first ten minutes.

Then I'd hand you a tray and give you something harmless to sort while I work.

I'd make tea, we'd probably argue about whether the radio should be on, and eventually you'd get used to the clocks ticking everywhere.

Honestly, that sounds like a pretty good evening to me.

choices.choiceText: Holding pegwood sticks and drinking smoky tea in a clock basement? That's my dream date.

nodes.partnerMessage:
No, I actually like it.

At first you hear thirty separate clocks. After a while you stop separating them and they become one soft background sound.

It's probably the closest thing I have to white noise.

Much better than waking up to a phone notification.

choices.choiceText: An ocean of brass waves. Let's step into your private feed so I can hear it.

nodes.partnerMessage:
That might be the real danger, yes.

Without a screen in front of us, we'd actually have to look at each other.

I'm not sure whether that's comforting or terrifying.

Probably a bit of both.

choices.choiceText: That's the whole point, Zephyrine. Show me the workshop.

nodes.partnerMessage:
There is room.

I'll move the brass shavings and make space beside the tools.

You can have the less comfortable chair. That's how I know I'm serious about you.

Come sit with me for a while.

We don't have to make the evening into anything bigger than it is.

choices.choiceText: Unlocking your workshop door right now.

nodes.partnerMessage:
The loupe is off.

Funny how different the room looks without it.

I spend so much time staring at things ten times larger than they really are that sometimes I forget to look at the person right in front of me.

I'm glad you're here.

choices.choiceText: You won't lose me. Give me the key to your Line feed.

nodes.partnerMessage:
That actually sounds good to me.

Tea, old clocks, brass shavings everywhere, and somebody I don't have to impress.

I don't need a fancy restaurant.

I'd rather spend an evening somewhere that already feels like mine and let you into it a little.

choices.choiceText: Entering your workshop now, Zephyrine.

nodes.partnerMessage:
The app makes the tiny details look terrible anyway.

I have a private bench feed where I post the close-up work, restoration notes, and the things I'm actually experimenting with.

It's much easier to show you the movement properly there.

Come have a look.

choices.choiceText: Taking the link. Meet me at your bench.

nodes.partnerMessage:
I've unlocked the workshop feed.

There are microscope views, restoration notes, and a few pieces I've never posted publicly.

Come inside, {PlayerName}.

I'll show you the parts of my world that don't fit neatly into a profile.

Can I ask you something that has nothing to do with watches?

What are you like when you actually have a free evening?

I spend so much time talking about my work that I realize I haven't asked what you do when nobody needs anything from you.

choices.choiceText: Honestly? I like quiet evenings too. Good food, a long conversation, and no need to be anywhere.
Why do I get the feeling you don't actually know how to take a night off either?

nodes.partnerMessage:
That sounds dangerously compatible with me.

I don't need constant plans. A good meal, somewhere quiet, and someone I can actually talk to is enough.

I think people confuse being quiet with being boring. They aren't the same thing.

choices.choiceText: Exactly. The best conversations usually happen when neither person is trying to impress the other.

nodes.partnerMessage:
That's fair.

I was probably going to say I take nights off, then immediately admit I sometimes bring a pocket movement home because I want to "just check one thing."

It is a problem.

choices.choiceText: So you're telling me you need somebody to confiscate your tools at bedtime.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yes. Exactly.

I think that's why this feels easier than I expected. I don't feel like I have to give you some carefully rehearsed version of myself.

I can just tell you that my tea is getting cold and my shoulder hurts and somehow that feels more intimate than trying to sound fascinating.

choices.choiceText: Good. Keep being honest with me. That's the version I want to know.

nodes.partnerMessage:
You joke, but that might actually work.

There are times when I realize it's two in the morning and I've been staring at the same wheel for forty minutes because I don't want to admit I'm tired.

Someone saying, "Put it away. Tomorrow exists too." would probably help.

choices.choiceText: Then I'll be the person who reminds you tomorrow still exists.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Then here's something ordinary.

I drink my tea too strong, I leave books open face-down even though I know I'm ruining them, and I have exactly one sweater I wear whenever I'm working because the sleeves don't catch on anything.

That's about as unromantic as I can get.

choices.choiceText: That's exactly the kind of thing I want to know. The ordinary stuff.

nodes.partnerMessage:
I like that.

People talk about dates as if everything has to feel extraordinary. I'm starting to think I'd rather have someone who makes an ordinary Tuesday feel easy.

That sounds much more sustainable to me.

choices.choiceText: Then let's start with an ordinary Tuesday and see where it goes.

nodes.partnerMessage:
One more thing.

I told you about my grandfather, but not really what he was like. He was stubborn, quiet, and terrible at admitting when he was proud of me.

Whenever I finished a repair, he'd just look at the movement, nod once, and say, "Good. Do it again tomorrow."

I miss that more than the praise itself.

choices.choiceText: That sounds like the kind of person whose approval meant a lot because he didn't give it away easily.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Exactly.

He taught me that love doesn't always look dramatic. Sometimes it's somebody putting your tools back where you left them because they know you'll need them in the morning.

I think I've carried that idea into relationships too.

choices.choiceText: So you notice the small things.

nodes.partnerMessage:
I do. Probably too much.

I notice when someone's voice changes, when they stop finishing their coffee, when they keep checking the door because they're nervous.

It can make dating difficult.

But with you, I don't feel like I'm constantly trying to interpret what you're not saying.

choices.choiceText: Then I'll try to tell you the truth instead of making you guess.

nodes.partnerMessage:
I'd like that.

I'm actually not looking for mystery anymore. I've had enough of people acting interesting because they refuse to be clear.

I'd rather know where I stand, even if the answer is simple.

choices.choiceText: Then here's the simple version: I like talking to you, and I want to see you again.
